Play cards from your hands in singles, doubles, triples, quads, or 3-card runs. There are no suits, and ranks can shift by clever manipulation of a 'conveyor belt' queue of cards. Whichever rank is in the rightmost position of the conveyor belt is the highest rank, and the ordering of the remaining ranks shifts according to a circular ranking. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Round Start 3 On Your Turn 4 Game End 5 Variant 5.1 Hickory Overview There are 48 cards (rank 1-12, 4 each) in the deck. Generally, the rank from low to high is from 1 to 12. But players will reposition the dickory board in the game. Round Start Shuffle the deck and deal 11 cards to each player. Place 6 card on the middle as queue . The rightmost card in queue shows the highest rank. The dickory board will show the new order. On Your Turn The lead player must play a meld (combo). There are 5 meld types: - Single : 1 card - Double : 2 cards in the same rank - Triple : 3 cards in the same rank - Quadruple : 4 cards in the same rank - Run of 3 : Exactly 3 cards of consecutive rank. If you are not the lead player, you must do one of the following action: - Beat the previous meld : Play a meld with the same type with higher rank (The rank of a run is always determined by its rightmost card) - Take card(s) from the queue and beat the previous meld : You may take 1-5 cards from the right of the queue. You can never take the leftmost card on the queue (one card must left). Then you must beat the previous meld with the new rank order. - Pass and refill the queue : If there is more than one card in the queue, discard the rightmost. Then, add card(s) to the queue on their left until there are 6 cards. The last player that played a meld becomes the lead player and plays a meld. Game End Once a player clears their hand, the player score 1. Start a new round until a player reaches the target score. Variant In both variant, there are two additional melds: Run of 2 cards and Run of 4 cards Hickory In the cases outlined below, you may now alter the previous meld by adding one (1) card to it: - If the previous meld was a single, double, or triple, you can beat the previous meld by playing a higher ranking meld of the same type OR you may now add one card to the previous meld to form a double, triple, or quadruple. - If the previous meld was a single, run of 2, or run of 3, you can beat the previous meld by playing a higher ranking meld of the same type OR you may now add one card to make it a run of 2, run of 3, or run of 4. You CANNOT add a card to a quadruple or to a run of 4; you would have to beat these melds with a higher-ranking meld of the same type. [Rating: 1/10] There's a lot of games that fumble when you add cards back into your hand, but this one works by having the card values constantly change. But that might also be its weakness, having to rethink your hand's strength almost every single turn. Then add more cards to it, and see if it has any new strengths. It can be too exhausting compared to other climbing games, where you start by forming a plan and then attempt to execute it. Part of it is staring at that damn clock, it's clever but honestly not that intuitive to think 5 is the strongest time on it, but that might change in a minute!

[Rating: 4/10] The Playte version uses full foil cards, which makes the game harder to play depending on your lighting. Very strange choice for this kind of game. I like the spinny thing on the box, but the New Mill version is better for playability.

[Rating: 5/10] Provisional rating. Very cool, quick shedder for 2p that can be played with a regular deck.  Mogul Scale: 1/A.

[Rating: 5/10] Another 2-player climbing game this month, but this one I liked decidedly less than Crisps. The problem for me is the constantly shifting rank of what is the highest value came across as more confusing than intuitive. The game does try to help you understand it, but the idea didn't click with me and I'm not sure how much I want to invest in trying to make sense of it. Simply put, the constant recalculation was too much mental gymnastics to be fun.

[Rating: 5/10] The rotating high value card is a novel idea, and it elegantly solves for draw luck issues that plague some games. These are good things.  The risk/reward of fast-forwarding to the final card in the face-up row to stick your opponent, but at the expense of probably taking 2-4 cards, is also a neat little decision point in some rounds. More generally, novel standard deck games are always welcome. I enjoy following both of the designers here on BGG and in their design efforts, and indeed that's what led me to Dickory in the first place.
